cards.heading: Definition: associative trail
cards.question: What is an associative trail, and how is it built?
cards.answer: A named, persistent path through a collection, built by joining items in pairs — the user brings two items into view together, names the trail, and ties them with a mutual code written into both so either can summon the other instantly.

cards.heading: Mechanism: the symmetric join
cards.question: Where does the join's code live, and why does that make the link belong to the items rather than a catalog?
cards.answer: In blank code spaces on each of the two items, each recording the other's index number — so the link is traversable from either end and belongs to the items themselves, not to a central catalog.

cards.heading: Trails are a by-product, not a plan
cards.question: How are associative trails built, according to the concept?
cards.answer: While working, not planned in advance — a path is a by-product of the inquiry itself (e.g. comparing bows, branching onto elasticity when materials turn out to matter), not a separate cataloguing task.

cards.heading: Trails compose rather than partition
cards.question: How can one item participate in a collection's organization under this scheme, compared to a filing system?
cards.answer: One item can sit on many trails at once, so paths compose rather than partition the collection the way a single filing scheme would.

cards.heading: A trail as a transferable artifact
cards.question: What becomes possible once a trail can be copied whole into another person's store, per the original proposal?
cards.answer: A profession of 'trail blazers' who establish useful paths through the common record, and an inheritance from a teacher that includes the whole scaffolding of reasoning behind their conclusions, not just the conclusions themselves.

cards.heading: Origin: a 1945 mechanical proposal
cards.question: What was the associative trail's original proposed mechanism, and what is it now considered the ancestor of?
cards.answer: A 1945 proposal (Vannevar Bush's memex) built on microfilm and photocells — it is the direct ancestor of hypertext and of every linked-note system since.
